Mr. Speaker, I raise a point of order in connection with this amendment, on the ground that yesterday the ruling made by the Chair was to the effect that any member whose privileges may be involved in a matter of this kind is obliged to ask leave of the house himself, or some other member may ask on his behalf.
Surely the first element of the situation is a request to an hon. member to appear and give

Question of Privilege
evidence, and I suggest that the ruling yesterday made it quite clear that it is open to an hon. member to decide for himself whether he wishes to give evidence before an inquiry on the debates and proceedings in the House of Commons. I do not dispute the right of the hon. member for Yukon or indeed his decision in this respect, but if he had chosen not to give evidence concerning the debates and proceedings that had taken place in the House of Commons he would have been within his rights to appear before the commission and refuse to do so.
I suggest that if the hon. member for Yukon had taken that course, his wish in this regard would have been respected by the courts, as it was in the only other known case that has taken place in this country. The hon. member for Yukon chose of his own volition to give evidence on the debates and proceedings here. In order to make absolutely sure that after he had given evidence no other member could accuse him of a breach of privilege, he has come to the house and asked for leave.
I suggest it is improper for any hon. member to make a decision with respect to this matter, in the first place on behalf of another member, who must decide for himself whether he wishes to give evidence on the debates and proceedings of this house. That is the first impropriety in the motion. The second is that it is improper, in the light of the ruling yesterday, for the hon. member for Greenwood to seek to give leave to hon. members who have not requested leave. It is improper to ask the house to give leave to members who have not been asked to appear before the commission, thus arrogating to the house a decision which is a matter of privilege for a member himself.
I suggest that in the light of the very clear ruling yesterday in respect of this matter, this amendment cannot be put because it is out of order.

subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-MOTION RESPECTING APPEARANCE BEFORE DORION COMMISSION
speechtext:
In other words, the reason for this privilege is that the freedom of a member of parliament shall not be circumscribed. The reason we have a motion such as this, and an amendment in order to clear up the position of others who may find themselves called, is to assure that the rights of parliament shall be preserved.
I heard hon. gentlemen opposite jeer a moment ago. This is not a jeering matter. This is something that is of foremost and preeminent importance to the preservation of parliament. If Your Honour has read the Duncan Sandys case you will have noticed it was made perfectly clear that if a representative in parliament could be called as a witness, that person could be placed in a position where an autocratic government would have him called so as to ascertain, through the medium of evidence, the source

of his information. To allow members of parliament to be cross-examined as to the sources of their information would place them in a position of subservience and would deny them that freedom which is essential to membership in parliament.
I take as an example the Sandys case. It was made perfectly clear that the privilege is not the privilege of the individual. A member receives information; someone passes information on to him. What would happen if our freedom were interfered with in that connection so that we could be cross-examined on the sources of our information? We would immediately close our sources of information, and in closing them would deny parliament its complete and absolute freedom of speech.
This is important to parliament. I doubt if at any time during my time here, and I have been here quite a long while, has there been a motion before the house more important than this one, not only to the present parliament but to parliaments that will follow hereafter. It deals with the maintenance above all else of the freedom of parliament, the assurance of freedom of speech which must not be limited in any way by subpoenas issued outside the house. To admit that that were possible would simply give to a tyrannical government-and I am not in any way indicating this one is in that position-to a tyrannical government less beneficent and benign than the present one, a challenging right over the freedom of members of parliament and, as such, a subversion of parliament. Therefore I submit the subamendment is well taken in every way. It is a most helpful and generous action.
The Prime Minister should have moved this motion. He refused, and now private members of parliament have had to do the work which he should have done.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. C. Munro (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: MR. MUNRO-UNAUTHORIZED REPRODUCTION OF OFFICIAL HOUSE DOCUMENT
speechtext:
I also desire to raise a question of privilege involving all members of this house, one which concerns the integrity and impartiality of your own position, Mr. Speaker, as custodian of the rules and rights of this house.
I have in my possession a document, Mr. Speaker, which closely allies your name and the imprint of your position with an unworthy

Question of Privilege
and partisan purpose. The document was published by Hamilton political action committee on behalf of a party represented in this house. I refer to the New Democratic party. A copy is in my possession, and I am raising the point of privilege at the earliest possible time.
On an inside page of the document, under the heading "Who is working for you?", appears an actual photographic reproduction of the front page of what is commonly known as the Hansard index, which as all hon. members are aware is an official publication of this house. This reproduction bears the coat of arms of Canada, along with the authority of you, Mr. Speaker, in your capacity as Speaker, and the imprint of the queen's printer. The inference, Mr. Speaker, is that this portion of the document was printed with the official sanction of this house, and I believe is a flagrant abuse of the prerogatives of parliament and a serious reflection on the office of Speaker.
I contend, Mr. Speaker, that a precedent was set in 1960 which supports my belief that this document constitutes a prima facie case of abuse of the rights and privileges of this house. You will recall that on February 16, 1960 the then C.C.F. member for Timmins, now the N.D.P. member for the same riding (Mr. Martin), raised a point of privilege about a similar use, or abuse, of official Commons documents. This precedent involved the photographic reproduction of the cover of Hansard, bearing the coat of arms and the authority of the Speaker and the queen's printer; as in this case, the reproduction was made for non-official propaganda purposes by a private organization.
The debate of February 15, 1960, page 1055 and February 16, pages 1100 to 1104, expresses the almost unanimous view of the house that a prima facie case of abuse of house privileges had been established in this earlier case to which I referred. Indeed, the Speaker of the day ruled that this was in fact the case. The prime minister of the day, now the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker), expressed the view that-
-your authority, Mr. Speaker, is called into issue inferentially.
He conceded that a breach had been committed, but he questioned whether it was serious enough to require definite action. This comment is found at page 1101 of Hansard for February 16, 1960. He added that the document-
-might tend to imply that the Speaker has authorized the publication of the document in question-
In the same debate the former member for Burnaby-Coquitlam stated that the photographic reproduction involved "the high office" of the Speaker and "the prestige of the coat of arms of Canada" in a base propaganda there was a prima facie case of breach of our rules and privileges in this house. This argument was further supported by the present member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch).
The Speaker of the day ruled that in fact there was a prima facie case of breach of privilege inasmuch as-
-this appears to be an official report published under the name of your Speaker-
He stated that:
-anything that relates to control by the house present or future over its own reports, having the possibility of abuse of such publications in mind- which is easily imaginable-requires me to allow this matter to go forward by finding at least prima facie grounds for complaint.
This ruling will be found at page 1104 of Hansard for February 16, 1960.
Mr. Speaker, your colleague of 1960 held that a question of privilege can be raised when "there is an abuse of the reports" of this house. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this reproduction is an abuse, not only because it reflects on the integrity and impartiality of you, Mr. Speaker, and your office, but because the matter is placed in a way which gives an unfair and misleading impression of the duties and activities of members of this house.
I might say that the primary basis upon which I advance this question of privilege is that it is an abuse of the rights and privileges of all members of this house. However, I do so also on a second ground, namely its highly misleading nature. The document is headed "Who is working for you?" and then follows an actual reproduction of the front page of the Hansard index, with, Mr. Speaker, as I say, your name as Speaker and the queen's printer imprint thereon. Then is shown a photostated reprint of the index in Hansard under each particular member's name, which is a course leading to nothing else but the inference that whoever should have the most references under his name in Hansard is the one who is working the hardest. Especially, Mr. Speaker, is it misleading when a goodly portion of the references here are to questions which have been placed on the order paper. Any hon. member can stay at home and never come to parliament, merely for-
[Mr. Munro.l

warding such questions to the house and having them put on the order paper.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Macaluso):
That the subject matter of this complaint be referred to the standing committee on privileges and elections for appropriate action.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF EXTENSION OF HOUSE BUILDING INCENTIVE PROGRAM

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF EXTENSION OF HOUSE BUILDING INCENTIVE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a statement on the winter house building incentive program. As hon. members know, we have been keeping a constant watch on the completion of housing under the winter house building incentive program with a view to determining whether or not an extension of the period for completion would be justified.
Last winter, because of shortages of materials and certain classes of skilled labour, the final inspection date of housing under the program was extended to April 15. This was done because the very success of the program had made it difficult for many builders to complete their housing units earlier.
This year the program commenced on November 15, which was 15 days earlier than last winter's program and, as a consequence of this adjustment in the program period, the situation in respect of the supply of material and labour has been much improved. My information is that there have been no shortages of building supplies and that, apart from

House Building Program-isolated shortages of specially skilled workers in the finishing trades, there has generally been a sufficient supply of construction labour.	:
There has been, however, this winter some exceptionally severe weather in certain parts of the country which has had the effect of delaying construction of some housing units under the program. I have received many representations from builders, as have other members of parliament, requesting an extension of the program mainly because of these severe weather conditions. On the other hand I have received representations from some builders with large housing projects requesting that the program not be extended.
On balance, however, having regard to the weather conditions which prevailed in many areas, I am pleased to announce that the period for completion of housing under this winter's program is being extended to April 15, 1965 in accord with a request made by the national house builders.
Mr. Speaker, it is the government's intention to place before the house an item in the supplementary estimates for the fiscal year 1965-66 to authorize this extension of the program.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF EXTENSION OF HOUSE BUILDING INCENTIVE PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF EXTENSION OF HOUSE BUILDING INCENTIVE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the numerous representations that have been made, not only to the government but to members of the opposition, to the effect that this program is not in effect for a sufficiently long period of time to enable builders to complete homes in accordance with the specifications set out by the government, the government has now acceded to the request which has been made, so these people will now qualify for the $500 bonus. I think greater success could be achieved under this program if the government saw fit now-and this may be something that the Minister of Finance could take into consideration when he is preparing the budget which he expects to bring down shortly-to eliminate the 11 per cent sales tax which the government imposed on construction materials, which has brought the price up and has caused the cost of living to rise, creating inflation to some extent in this country.
This program cannot be classified as one which has proven to be a success. It is true that in the first year, and I give these figures from memory, some 35,000 units were completed, but there was not a substantial increase over that number in the second year, at which time, because of the success of the program,


the figures should have indicated that more and more people participated. I think the figures show that the number of units built under this program in the second year was almost identical to the number in the first year.
This program has been much less successful than the municipal winter works incentive program, which has shown an increase in each and every year. That program was started by the previous government when it was in office and is being carried on successfully at the present time. Unless some other incentive is provided to the housing program, such as the elimination of the 11 per cent sales tax on building material, there will be a decreasing number of participants in the coming winter.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF EXTENSION OF HOUSE BUILDING INCENTIVE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of this party welcome the minister's announcement. It is undoubtedly true that weather conditions this year have been particularly severe in many parts of Canada, and it is only fair and proper that the winter housing program should be extended until April 15, but I am not suggesting for a moment that this will solve all the housing problems. If the government really wants to stimulate housing the first thing it could do would be to remove the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials. Nevertheless, this extension will help to prevent certain hardships being placed on individuals who through no fault of their own have been unable to proceed far enough with their winter house construction programs to benefit from the program.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that all the arguments which have convinced the Minister of Labour to extend this winter house building program to April 15 apply equally to an extension of the winter works incentive program, because the same bad weather which made it difficult to get housing starts under way and advanced to the point where they will be completed by a set date applied even more to the municipal winter works incentive programs. A great many of the municipalities, as part of their winter works incentive programs, have been laying sewer and water lines. This type of work is extremely difficult during the type of winter we have had, particularly in the past few months. Therefore I would hope that the minister, who has kindly acceded to this extension of the date with reference to winter housing, will now seriously consider extending the date in respect of the winter works incentive program, particularly because it affects so many municipalities and areas of Canada.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF EXTENSION OF HOUSE BUILDING INCENTIVE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in the Social Credit party are grateful that the minister has seen fit to make this announcement in respect of the 15 day extension to the winter house building incentive program. On a number of occasions during the last two months I have brought the situation in this regard to his attention. Great difficulty and hardship have been worked not only upon those people in the business of building houses but also upon those individuals who are going to own those homes, in that they have geared their financial positions in respect of down payments and initial costs to the fact that there is a $500 bonus available. I am sure this announcement will be received with considerable satisfaction across the country.
I should also like to state that we have now reached almost the end of March and the deadline is drawing near, and it would have been helpful if this announcement had been made several weeks ago.
I join with the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam in urging the government to extend the winter works incentive program in a similar manner, because I realize that a number of municipalities, cities and towns are in great difficulty as a result of extreme weather conditions which, incidentally, still exist at the present time in many parts of the country. It is equally imperative that the government extend this program.
I realize that these programs are partly aimed at encouraging winter employment. Nevertheless, to deny either municipalities or home owners the opportunity to participate in the financial benefits which accrue will also work a hardship upon them, so I again urge upon the minister the need to consider a similar extension to the winter works program as far as municipalities are concerned.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF EXTENSION OF HOUSE BUILDING INCENTIVE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we were also glad to hear the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) announce that the period of winter works would be extended until April 15 as concerns housing construction. Many builders will benefit from this 15 day extension, but I wonder if the minister, while deciding upon this extension, took into consideration the designated areas which also encountered very cold temperatures, not only in a particular district, but in many others?
Furthermore, did the minister examine the situation which exists in unorganized par-
House Building Program ishes, that is, in parishes which are not constituted as municipalities? The minister well knows that in those unorganized parishes, winter works did not start on the first of November or December last, nor even on January 1 last, because the federal government wished the municipal council or councils held responsible for the carrying out of those winter works, whether in a designated area or not. I believe that the officials of the Department of Labour then were not up to the situation, and today many unorganized parishes are requesting a further extension beyond the one which was granted.
I come from a designated area, an underdeveloped area, and the minister has no solution to offer toward solving the problems which face many unorganized parishes in my riding, and also parishes in my neighbouring riding, Pontiac-Temiscamingue.
While I appreciate that this 15 day extension will allow large builders to receive the $500 bonus, this does not help labour in unorganized parishes, which could not start their projects sooner, because the present government did not assume its responsibilities.
Mr. Speaker, it must be recognized, as pointed out earlier by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) and the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr), that instead of giving a $500 bonus for each house built, in order to help the Canadian consumer the 11 per cent sales tax should be abolished. As a matter of fact, this 11 per cent sales tax on building materials easily eats up twice the amount of $500 handed out by the federal government for every house built. I think it does not make any sense.
On the one hand I can understand the government being proud to say that houses are going up everywhere but, on the other hand, the 11 per cent tax-and the finance minister is perfectly aware of the situation- eliminates, as it were, twice the amount of $500 granted on each house built.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a question-which 
I always like doing-to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In view of reports that the Prime Minister's efforts to bring about a cessation of hostilities in Viet Nam have failed, and in view of the news with respect to the stepping up of the situation there, the use of gas and so on, would the minister mind telling the house what the government proposes to do to meet this situation from this point on?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: VIET NAM-INQUIRY AS TO PROPOSED GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend's question seems to be predicated on the belief that the only country with responsibilities in this matter is Canada. My hon. friend will of course recognize that Canada is not one of the combating countries, that we are one of the 14 power group, and that we are doing everything we can to bring about a cease fire. But the fact is, as both the British prime minister and his foreign secretary yesterday in Washington have said, that at this moment, notwithstanding the appeal made by Britain, one of the co-chairmen, to the Soviet union, the latter refuses to move toward a cease fire, presumably on the ground that there is no evidence that Hanoi is disposed to a cease fire or that Hanoi has had any encouragement toward this objective by communist China.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: VIET NAM-INQUIRY AS TO PROPOSED GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. May I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether his attention has been drawn to the fact that a former military adviser on the international control commission in Viet Nam, Colonel Bradley Webb, stated- and he is now, by the way, the secretary of the Canadian institute of international affairs -in Toronto at a public meeting that there has been no significant infiltration of North Vietnamese communist troops or equipment into South Viet Nam. He said this was certainly true until a few months ago, and there is no reason to believe differently now. It seems to me that this statement by one who has been on the actual scene of operations and who was formerly a member of the truce commission staff is completely at variance with the statements which the minister has constantly reiterated in this house.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: VIET NAM-INQUIRY AS TO PROPOSED GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend has raised an important matter. I know he would not want to give the impression that the colonel in question was a commissioner, because he was not; he was a military officer serving the commission, and he was there only for a limited period. I can

only say to him that the incontrovertible evidence is as stated by the majority of the commission in 1962, made up of Canada and India. We have no reason to doubt the authenticity of the facts assessed and presented by the representatives of Canada through the recent minority report. The views in question are those of one man who was in Indochina for a limited period. I am satisfied from the evidence I have seen that both the 1962 and the 1965 reports present a balanced picture.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: VIET NAM-INQUIRY AS TO PROPOSED GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: A supplementary question. Is it not equally true that Canada in 1962, in signing the report along with India, declared that South Viet Nam and the United States were violating the agreement, and that the situation which obtained at that time has not changed; if anything, it has grown worse. The minister keeps reiterating one side of the report. It seems to me that he ought at the same time to remind the house and the country that Canada also recognized the violations of the Geneva accord by both South Viet Nam and the United States.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: VIET NAM-INQUIRY AS TO PROPOSED GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. friend put this question in another form last week. Canada did not dispute the facts in the majority report; but this does not alter the fact that the conclusions of the minority report are substantiated and are not in any way thwarted by the conclusions of the majority report. North Viet Nam is engaged in fighting and infiltrating in the south. Whether or not my hon. friend fully concurs in the conclusions as to how this happened, this is the case. The commission points out that the first act of aggression by the north occurred shortly after the Geneva conference of 1954.
We join with other countries in hoping there will be a cease fire. But the evidence now available clearly imposes an unanswerable responsibility on North Viet Nam and on any country that may be supporting her. I am sure that the position of most countries in the Geneva accord group, including the Soviet union, is that there should be a cessation of hostilities. Any indication that there is a willingness on the part of Hanoi to bring this about will, I think, meet with response.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, March 16, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-136, to establish a comprehensive program of old age pensions and supplementary benefits in Canada payable to and in respect of contributors-Miss LaMarsh-Mr. Lamou-reux in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Order. House in committee of the whole on Bill No. C-136, to establish a comprehensive program of old age pensions and supplementary benefits in Canada payable to and in respect of contributors.
On clause 1-Short title.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, while we were on second reading last November I made a few general remarks with regard to the Canada pension plan. During the clause by clause discussion in the committee of the whole I also made reference to specific provisions in the bill. We are now on clause 1 and I should like to make a few general remarks about the ambit of the Canada pension plan.
[Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria).!
This is indeed important legislation. To give an idea of the scope of the legislation, with regard to cost it has been estimated that the collections by way of contributions would represent an increase of about 23 per cent in income tax. It is truly said that this is probably one of the most important pieces of social legislation which has been introduced in this house. Unfortunately, I find in many parts of Canada that people have been misled about what the Canada pension plan would do for them.
First of all, I should like to go back to the last election campaign where the deception started. I have before me a half page advertisement from the Vancouver Sun dated April 4, 1963 which refers to pensions. This is an advertisement of the Liberal party which says, among other things:
-at age 70 the pension will be $296 for a couple or $231 for a single person.
A far cry, Mr. Chairman, from the provisions in this bill. Furthermore, this advertisement gives the impression that this is the pension which will apply to all people. While on the subject of this advertisement, a little lower down it says:
To help people already retired, who have not had a chance to contribute under the new Liberal plan, a minimum supplementary pension of $10 per month will be paid, from the start, out of the pension fund established by contributions.
We all know what happened in July, 1963 when the first Canada pension plan was introduced in the house. We moved that $10 be paid immediately. At that time every member on the other side voted against it; but in due course of time they were compelled by public opinion to finally grant the $10 which we had asked them to do at that time.
Another point I want to make is that our group both in committee and in this house tried to move an amendment whereby a flat minimum benefit of $25 would be paid under the Canada pension plan fund even to those people who did not contribute. One of the replies which were given by members on the other side was that this is a contributory pension plan, and that therefore those who did not contribute should not receive anything. Yet in their own advisement they said that $10 would be paid to everyone over 70 even if they had not contributed anything. So time has changed their minds in that respect, as it has changed their minds in many others.
I think a word might be in order about the usual fumbling and bumbling of this govern-

ment. We have become used to this with regard to almost everything that has been introduced, but I want to refer specifically to their fumbling and bumbling with regard to the Canada pension plan. The first plan was introduced in this house on July 18, 1963. At that time the Minister of National Health and Welfare indicated that it was entirely up to the house how expeditiously they treated this matter, but that this great creation will become law for the benefit of all Canadians. Well, Mr. Chairman, that plan died a quiet death.
Then in a second try, on March 17, 1964 the minister introduced another Canada pension plan, Bill No. C-75. This was her second offspring. Even at that time, Mr. Chairman, a white paper was being prepared, and the third Canada pension plan was born on August 10, 1964. There were a lot of difficulties and poor handling regarding the release of the actuarial reports, the appendices thereto, the economic report, and so on.
Then again, last week the members of the Creditistes raised the question of lack of translation of the minutes into French. Ministers and members on the other side said that it would take six months to have these translations completed. Then the following day the Prime Minister said that it would be done in six days. This is typical of the way the Canada pension plan and other legislation has been handled by this government.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I want to go into some of the shortcomings of the Canada pension plan, as I see it. I am indeed sorry that the member from Victoria (B.C.) is, as usual, not in his seat, because although I very much enjoyed addressing several organizations in his riding on the Canada pension plan I now have so many other requests that I may not be able to accommodate further requests from the riding of Victoria (B.C.) and I had hoped that he might be here to learn something about it so that he could fulfil his duty to his constituents.
The main shortcoming, Mr. Chairman, of the Canada pension plan, as I see it, is the inequity between various groups of Canadians. The first group I want to refer to are all those people who are now retired who will not get one penny benefit out of the Canada pension plan. The question immediately arises: By what valid reason, by what reason at all, does a government have a greater responsibility to those people who will be 20220-8031
Canada Pension Plan
retiring in the next few years than it has to those who are now retired?
The fact is, Mr. Chairman, that those individuals who are now retired will not receive one penny in benefits from the Canada pension plan. It may be that members on the other side will say that in due course these people will benefit, but let us consider what will happen in 1976 to this group who are now retired, after the plan has been in operation for ten years. In 1976, 66 per cent, of those people will not receive one penny in benefits from the Canada pension plan. Some 32 per cent of these people will receive average benefits in the amount of $45 per month, and the fortunate 1.5 per cent of the group will receive an average of $119 per month.
This group of people is one that is probably in greatest need because they spent the greatest part of their earning lives during the depression and pre-war periods when wages were very low; yet they will not receive one penny in benefits from the plan. Even in 1980 when the plan will have been in operation for almost 15 years more than half of the people in this group, and there will be something like 1,800,000 of them, will not receive one penny from the Canada pension plan. In spite of the fact that there will be this group receiving nothing, there will be another fortunate group of Canadians who will receive very large windfalls. For example, an individual who has contributed for only ten years and then retires at age 65 will receive a bonus and the windfall portion of that bonus, or the unearned part, will amount to over $18,000.
Another group of Canadians will not receive benefits, or very low benefits, from the plan, and I refer to that group who consistently earn less than the minimum required under the provisions of the bill, being $600 per year for an employed individual and $800 a year for a self-employed individual. I have taken extracts from the dominion bureau of statistics reports in this regard. According to the 1961 census there were
369.000	Canadian wage earners who earned less than $500 per year. There were over
700.000	Canadian wage earners who earned less than $1,000 a year. These are the groups of Canadian wage earners whose records of earnings are the most erratic of any in Canada, and these are the ones who will receive practically nothing, or nothing, from the Canada pension plan. These are the people who, because of their low earnings,

Canada Pension Plan
will not be able to set anything aside for their retirement, and when the time arrives for them to retire they will quite properly look to their communities to help them. The Canada pension plan will not help them to any great extent.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
The hon. member will permit questions after he has completed his speech, if there is enough time.
Perhaps this is an opportune time to refer to what the minister of national health said when she introduced the first plan in this house in July 1963. She said that the purpose of this government proposed legislation was to ensure that as soon as it is possible to make the plan effective, in a practical way, all Canadians will be able to retire in security and with dignity. That is the principle for which we voted on the motion for second reading. But does the Canada pension plan accomplish that principle?
The group consistently earning less than $600 per year and the group of self-employed individuals earning less than $800 per year consists, in the main, of farmers and fishermen. I have some figures in relation to the earnings of fishermen in certain provinces and I hope that all hon. members representing constituencies in Newfoundland, Quebec, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick will listen carefully to these figures, which refer to the average annual value of landed fish, per fisherman, in the years 1960 to 1962.
In Newfoundland, which has some 18,800 commercial fishermen, the average landed value of fish per fisherman was $850. From that figure they will have to deduct their expenses, so it is certain that the average fisherman in Newfoundland will not qualify for benefits under this plan.
The average landed value of fish per fisherman in Quebec in the period 1960 to 1962 was $875. In Prince Edward Island the average per fisherman was $1,345. Again from my general knowledge of fishing I would state that half of that value would go to expenses, so these fishermen will not qualify. In New Brunswick the average landed value of fish per fisherman was $1,400. It is certain that the majority of fishermen in that province will not benefit under this plan. Surely the majority of small farmers in Quebec and in the eastern provinces will not benefit in any way, or in a very small way, from the Canada pension plan.

Another shortcoming of the Canada pension plan is that for many years those people who earn the most money will receive the greatest bonus, while those who earn the least will receive the smallest bonus. For example, a self-employed person who retires in 1981, after the plan has been in operation for 15 years, and who contributes on the basis of average earnings of $5,000 a year, would receive a windfall to the extent of $20,000. That individual may well have earned $10,000 to $20,000 per year. Provided he earned at least $5,000 per year he would receive a windfall of $20,000. On the other hand, a person whose income was only half that, or $2,500, would be less able to provide for his retirement but would receive a bonus of only $10,000. Under the provisions of this plan the relationship of benefits to earnings progresses downward until it reaches the minimum, at which time the bonus becomes almost negligible.
Furthermore the discrepancy between what a person with a high income level will receive and what a person with a low income will receive is aggravated in the future by the provision for acceleration. For example an individual who receives the maximum, or $100 per month, if the consumer price index went up over a ten year period at 2 per cent per year, would receive $2 per month more. On the other hand, an individual whose pension was $20 per month would receive an increase of only 60 cents per month. After ten years the difference in increases between the pension of $104 per month and that of $20 per month would become not $82, but $100, so it can readily be seen that the escalation provisions of the bill will aggravate the discrepancy.
I should like to quote now from a recent issue of the Canadian Tax Journal to give an example of how an individual with a high income actually pays less to the government by way of contribution than a man with a small income. For example, a man with an income of $20,000 a year will pay only $43.45 per year toward the plan. This is because he is in the 45 per cent tax bracket and he is therefore able to deduct 45 per cent of the cost of his contribution. On the other hand, a person who has an income or gross salary of only $5,000 a year will pay the full contribution of $79 toward the plan.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question at that point?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
If you do not mind, no, because I have not got too much time. I will

be glad to take them afterwards. Write them down if you cannot remember them. I want to refer for a moment to the small businessmen, many of whom will be very hard hit by the Canada pension plan. I will describe one inequity brought to my attention by a small businessman. He is a trucker who operates two trucks and employs one man. This trucker's net income is $5,000 a year. He also pays his truck driver $5,000 a year. This small businessman will pay $240 a year toward the Canada pension plan while his employee will pay roughly $80 a year. In other words, the employer will pay three times what the employee pays but they will both get the same pension.
I want to refer to the position of married women. I had hoped that the Minister of National Health and Welfare might be a little more sympathetic toward them, but since she has not been I am afraid I will have to take up their cause for them. I contend that the Canada pension plan treats the married woman who stays home and minds the family very badly compared with others in other positions. For example, a young woman begins to work at age 20 and she works for 10 years with average earnings of $3,000 per year. After working for 10 years she gets married and looks after her children. When she finally reaches the age of 65 she is entitled to a pension and her pension will be about $15 per month. In other words, she has paid for 10 years on the basis of earnings of $3,000 per year.
Take the case of another woman who happens to be a little older. She is 55 and she pays exactly the same amount. She pays for 10 years based on an average annual salary of $3,000 per year but she gets a pension of $62 a month. In other words, although they both pay the same the woman who is 55 gets four times the pension of the other woman.
Here is another example of how the woman who minds her family is penalized, so to speak. Take the example of a married couple, both of whom are working. When they retire at age 65 they will have a combined pension, including old age security, of $350 a month. Take the case of the other woman who stayed home and minded her family. In due course the other married couple will retire with a pension of $100 a month less.
I have a few incidental points I want to make, the first having to do with students. Although in committee members voted unanimously for an increase in the drop-out provision, that is, the number of work years of their earning life they will be allowed to
Canada Pension Plan
eliminate, in the house the minister would not agree to anything more than 15 per cent. In our opinion this penalizes students. There is no doubt that Canada must do all in its power-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Order. I hesitate to interrupt the hon. member at this stage because I recognize that he is probably the leadoff speaker on behalf of his party on clause 1. However, I think I should caution the hon. member who is speaking now, as well as other hon. members who intend to take part in the debate, that although our practice of recent years, which is contrary to the written rule of the committee, has been to allow discussion of a general nature on clause 1, there are still limitations to what hon. members can consider. One of them, of course, is that we cannot go outside the contents of the bill itself, and another is that whenever a decision has been arrived at in the committee with regard to a particular clause it is very doubtful if it is possible for hon. members to revive the subject matter of that clause, because obviously that would reflect on the vote of the committee. We have an upsidedown procedure when we are studying clause 1 following consideration of the other clauses of the bill, and I know it will cause difficulties in the course of the discussion. This is perhaps the first time that the new rule approved and recommended by the committee on procedure and organization is being tried out. I know it may cause difficulties, but certainly the point should be kept in mind that whenever a decision has been reached by the committee on a particular clause discussion of that clause should not be reopened. I am sure my hon. friend will keep that in mind.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I did not mean to reflect on the decision of the committee with regard to the 15 per cent. I merely wanted to point out that in my opinion this does adversely affect students who may spend six, seven or more years of their lives at a university and will have used up their total dropout entitlement. If they retire earlier than 65 they will have no more years they can use for dropout purposes since they have used them all up.
Another difficulty in regard to the Canada pension plan is the tremendously complicated nature of the plan. Not only is it complicated to understand in the first place but I think the real difficulty with regard to the complications of the plan will arise in due course when people try to understand it. I do not

Canada Pension Plan
see how the average, ordinary employee or self-employed person, unless he has expert advice, will have any idea what his pension is going to be. It will be almost impossible to find out, and certainly I think it is elementary that any person, particularly when he gets to the point where he is approaching retirement, wants to know what his pension is going to be when he retires. In his earlier years he also wants to know what other provision he might make for his retirement, but the fact is that he will have very little idea of what his pension will be when he reaches 65.
I want to make a brief reference to the opting out provision of the bill. I think the real difficulty of the government arises by virtue of the fact that they went into the Canada pension plan and promised the people a national pension plan without due consideration of section 94A of the British North America Act, which reads as follows:
The parliament of Canada may make laws in relation to old age pensions and supplementary benefits, including survivors' and disability benefits irrespective of age, but no such law shall effect the operation of any law present or future of a provincial legislature in relation to any such matter.
Therefore the government had no option in its approach to this whole matter of allowing a province to opt out. Of course, once a province has opted out it can, by virtue of the British North America Act, change the plan in any way it wants. In this regard I should like to quote one or two statements from an address made by Hon. John Robarts, prime minister of Ontario, in the legislature on January 21, 1965. With reference to the question of whether the government of Ontario should opt out he said:
On the other hand, the province of Ontario and this government have traditionally worked for national unity and national standards of social services. We have participated in national social security programs and in many other instances have provided support in the interests of national standards and national stability.
Here is the pertinent sentence:
In the present circumstances, if we were to propose a plan in which there were any marked differences, even though "comparable", we might seriously impair the principle of national portability of pensions, which has been one of our goals for many years.
The premier distinctly recognizes the fact that any province which opts out has the right to change the plan in any way it wishes, and I think it is obvious that once such a plan is changed, then portability across Canada or between that province and
[Mr. Chatterton.l
the other provinces that have not opted out could well be destroyed. I quote another sentence from the remarks of the premier of Ontario. Referring to his decision to stay with the Canada pension plan he said:
In coming to this decision, I am well aware that the government of Quebec has indicated that it intends to administer its own pension plan, which will be comparable to the Canada pension plan and, it is hoped, will not seriously impair interprovincial portability.
He went on to say:
While I can sympathize with this decision I nevertheless do not despair that in the future the government of Quebec may see fit to enter into the national plan, which will be so similar to its own. If this could come to pass, we would achieve our ultimate goal of a truly national pension plan that would go far toward setting the pattern for future, nation-wide, social welfare legislation.
I think it is trying to mislead the people of Canada to say that this is necessarily a national Canada pension plan, as it is quite possible that because of the whole approach of this government it may not be portable in every part of Canada. I wish to say just a word about the integration of private pension plans with the Canada pension plan. As the minister said and as the bill indicates, the Canada pension plan does not in any way affect any pension plan that is in existence now, and if there is to be any change it is up to the private pension plan to integrate or adjust.
I submit that the evidence given before the joint committee indicates that, primarily because the Canada pension plan is not funded on an actuarially sound basis, it will be extremely difficult for private pension plans to properly integrate. Just to give an example, the government itself has of now, I presume, found out this difficulty and they are now working on amendments to the Public Service Superannuation Act so that it will be integrated with the Canada pension plan. The government has announced in general terms its formula for amending or integrating the P.S.S.A. into the Canada pension plan. I would just quote one example of an anomaly that occurs in this integration. This is with regard to widows' pension. I have looked up two examples here where a widow receives a pension actually greater than the salary of her husband before he died. I quote one of these cases, where the average salary of the husband in the civil service was $3,000 per year-that is, the average of his best six years. He would receive a pension after 35 years service of $2,100. His widow's pension under the P.S.S.A. would be $1,050 a year, and for four children the pension would be $840 a

a year. Under the Canada pension plan that widow would receive $580, and for four children she would receive $1,200. In other words, the widow's pension in that case would be $3,670, which is 122 per cent of her husband's salary at the date of his demise. This shows the difficulties in integrating any private pension plan with the Canada pension plan.
I predict, Mr. Chairman, that in future the Canada pension plan will be a political football. A huge fund will be built up of up to $8.5 billion by 1985, and yet large groups of Canadians, particularly those with the greatest need, will receive no benefit or very little benefit from the Canada pension plan. Therefore it is the most natural thing in the world for these people to put pressure on politicians in order to receive some benefit from this fund, particularly when it is said that it will not cause any immediate increase in taxation. Now, Mr. Chairman, a word with regard to part IV of Bill No. C-136.

As I have said on a previous occasion, I believe that if the government intends to make the old age security pension available at age 65, it should be done at the same time. It is going to be very difficult for people who are now 65 years of age to understand why they do not get the old age security pension, whereas in 1970 those who are 65 years of age will receive the old age security pension.
I now wish to say a word or two about our proposals in the committee. We recommended that all those now 70 years of age and over who are in receipt of old age security pension should receive $25 a month out of the Canada pension plan. We suggested that those between 65 and 70 years of age who are retired should also receive $25 a month from the Canada pension plan. Furthermore we felt that all those who regularly earn less than

the minima described in the bill and who would normally get no pension, or a very small pension under the Canada pension plan, should receive $25 a month minimum pension for a single person and $40 a month for a married couple. Our group was the only one that voted for this recommendation in the committee.
I believe that the government should have approached this whole question of pensions in the way it was approached in 1952 when there was a joint committee on this subject. That committee was not told, "Here is the plan; please rubber stamp it". They were told to determine what was the best type of plan that should be introduced, and they came up with the old age security without the means test. I believe that if a similar approach had been taken and the government had sent this plan to the committee before second reading, that would have helped. I believe that if this approach had been taken, the plan with which we are dealing at the present time might have been materially different.

Mr. Chairman, I have no intention of reviewing or repeating arguments expressed on both sides of the house as to the benefits or lack of benefits of this plan. The minister will be pleased to know that I have no intention of speaking on the opting out provision, because I am completely satisfied that everyone in Canada will have equal benefits from the pension plan. But I would like to emphasize one aspect of the plan which has not been touched on in this committee, namely the economic advantage to be gained from it.
There are still many people, insurance companies and the like, adamantly opposed to the plan even though it has almost become law, and they have expressed many fears. I would like to say a word or two in order to belittle their apprehensions. It will be noted that life insurance sales increased last year even though this plan had been under consideration during that time. However, that did not stop people from buying life insurance, which has an element of pension in it. This furthers the argument that rather than being of no benefit to the private companies the plan will be an advantage to them. No doubt we shall have the same experience as in the United States, and sales of private pension plans will increase.
Another point I would like to mention is one which was well publicized in a chamber of commerce speech by Mr. Weldon, in which he said that the portability provision alone would more than pay for any cost of the plan. Most hon. members know that many employees are tied to their jobs or positions because of a pension plan, but if their pension plan becomes portable, the same as the Canada pension plan, they may change jobs and thus increase productivity. From experience I know of many men and women working in jobs they do not like, and thus do not give more than 10 per cent of their ability to them.
There are two other elements to be considered. We are all concerned about the fact that Canadians do not own shares in Canadian industry, and the cause is the apprehension they are subject to, of not knowing that will happen to them in their old age. Thus, when it comes to a question of taking

a risk and buying shares they are naturally apprehensive. A plan such as this, which envisions a fairly decent standard of living for people in their old age, will remove some of this apprehension, and thus people will invest more money during their productive years in buying shares.
Even if the people who now own shares in our industries made those shares available to Canadians at half price there would not be sufficient Canadians to buy them, due mainly the fact that they are apprehensive about their declining years. Eventually, due to this plan people will be able to buy more shares, and the money which will remain in Canada accruing from the profits and dividends will more than offset any costs of the Canada pension plan.
I emphasize these points because much has been made of the socialistic side of the plan, the social conscience involved, and the idea that this is a gift. It is not a gift. Anyone who looks at it from a business point of view will acknowledge it is an investment for the future, and by and large it will not be as expensive as might be imagined. Even if it is so expensive we can more than make up for that from the side effects of such a plan.

Mr. Chairman, I just wish to make a few general remarks on the legislation before us. Considerable attention has been given to it during clause by clause study. Members have had the opportunity to raise objections to certain clauses and to suggest amendments. But now we have reached this stage and we find very few consequential amendments were made to the measure, and in all probability it will be adopted pretty much in the form in which it was introduced.
Mention was made this afternoon about the portability provision. This is one of the most important proposals in the measure. We have reached a period in our history when it is absolutely necessary that provision be made so individuals can change from one job to another without in any way losing or jeopardizing their pension benefits. If portability were the only provision in this measure I think there would be wide acceptance of it, and wide appreciation for it.
A considerable investment fund is to be set up and placed at the disposal of the various provincial administrations. A question has been raised as to whether the plan should be used for such a purpose, whether it is right and proper that the money paid into the fund should be used in that fashion. I believe it will make a worth-while contribution to our economy because if the capital

needs of provincial and municipal governments can be satisfied from this fund, additional private capital will be left for investment in industry and business. I do not think we have anything to fear along that line. Further, use of the fund in this way will create additional job opportunities and the country's economy will benefit in the long run.
However, there is considerable apprehension about many aspects of the plan, and I would like to deal with some of those aspects. I am not so naive as to believe that any fundamental changes or amendments will be made to it, but I do want to voice some of the objections that have been brought to my attention.
First, there is the compulsory aspect of the plan, and this principle of compulsion is repugnant to all those who support the concept of individual initiative and responsibility. This seems to be another indication of the thinking of the government, that it does not believe people have the ability or intelligence to invest their money in order to provide for their retirement years. Therefore the government is making it compulsory that people pay into the Canada pension plan in order that they may receive some benefits from it during their declining years. I can appreciate the views of those who take strong exception to this compulsory aspect of it.
Therefore I believe we should consider whether there is not some other way to make this work effectively and adequately, without using force and compulsion to make people contribute to the plan.
Another objection is that it does not provide benefits for all Canadians, as was originally suggested. As has been pointed out, many of those in the greatest need of its provisions will not be eligible to participate in it. Therefore some have stated, possibly with justification, that this plan would be of greatest benefit to those who need it less than others who will be unable to take full advantage of its provisions. I believe that in future, in the light of experience, provision will have to be made to extend its scope to a greater number of people who are desirous of participating in this plan.
I believe it has been pointed out on a number of occasions that this is actually a form of increased taxation which will result in reduced take home pay. I do not believe that many people nowadays have too much money left in their hands; I think most people have little left over after providing for 20220-804
Canada Pension Plan
their basic needs. This plan will drain off an additional amount from the take home pay of Canadians across this country and is likely to place many of them in a difficult position, bearing in mind the continued increase in the cost of living and its effect on providing for the families of those who would be affected. The hon. member who spoke before me referred to what he called the economic advantages of this plan. I suggest that from a personal point of view there are bound to be definite economic disadvantages as a result of reduced take home pay-the smaller amount left with which to purchase the necessities of life.
There is another objection, and it is this: a person who has already provided for his own retirement and for the security of his survivors to the limit of his financial ability will now have to reorganize his arrangements in order to take care of these new requirements. I think this constitutes an imposition upon those who have shown initiative-and perhaps enjoyed advantages-which enables them to make provision for themselves. As a result of this bill they will have to disturb the whole set up, re-appraise their position and make the necessary changes in the arrangements they have made for retirement in order that this new plan which has been imposed on them may receive the necessary contributions. I do not think this is fair. I think it constitutes a penalty upon those who have had the foresight and the ability to make retirement provisions for themselves. As I mentioned a few moments ago, substantial amendments will no doubt have to be made in the light of experience in the operation of this plan. I do not think anyone will deny that, taking account of the fact that the plan is operating in an area which is relatively new. I suggest these amendments will need to be substantial and drastic; they will have to recognize some of the basic weaknesses and fundamental flaws in this whole scheme. I trust the government will make sure that these amendments are introduced the moment they are recognized as being necessary in order that the plan may work to the advantage of Canadians as a whole.
These are just a few observations. As I pointed out, I am not so naive as to expect that any fundamental changes will be made at this stage. However, we trust the minister will take note of the points which have been drawn to her attention by various members of this house and make sure that when the opportunity presents itself amendments will

Mr. Chairman, Bill No. C-136 establishing a Canada pension plan is made up of four parts; the first one deals with contributions, the second one with pensions and supplementary benefits, the third one with the administration of the plan and the fourth one with the amendments to the Old Age Security Act.
In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, that plan is a devious method used by the government to secure new funds to enable it to make ends meet each year.
The government's aim is not to pay a pension to people aged 65 or 70, and the Minister of National Health and Welfare admitted it herself, as well as other ministers, but to find between $5 and $7 billion within the next ten years.
It is clear that the pension paid at age 65 or 70 will not come from the money paid at the present time to the government by young people. When we reach age 65 or 70 this pension will be paid to us with the money collected from our children by the government. This is the purpose of the pension plan.
Instead of calling it a new tax a new name has been found for it; it is called a pension plan with a compulsory contribution, so that any Canadian will receive a pension in his old age. That, Mr. Chairman, amounts in fact to a national barbotte. It is nothing else but that.
And at the provincial level they want to set up a similar, identical and parallel pension plan.
That is why we advise the people of the province of Quebec who will be called upon to subscribe to a similar plan, independent to a certain extent of the national plan, but which must take into consideration the data or standards of the federal plan, to object firmly and positively to this pension plan which is but a confiscation of savings and salaries.
At a time when the national revenue is not high enough to purchase the national production of Canadians, the government brings forth this plan in order to draw' more from the pay envelopes of the workers and the people of Canada in general.
Within a few years, this pension plan will take away from wage earners a revenue of approximately $8 to $9 billion of the national revenue. That is what the pension

plan will take out of the national revenue within a few years.
The purpose of this plan is to find from $5 to $7 billion. Why always insist upon the fact that we will be helping Canadians who have attained the age of 65, whereas we will be fleecing them as long as they are working.
A youth who starts working at the age of 18 or 19 will contribute until he has reached the age of 65, and then, instead of reimbursing him the money he has paid, as I said a moment ago, the government will pay him a pension out of the contributions which his children will then be paying. Most likely, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) will not be here by then. Even the present government will not exist, it will have been replaced by another. The coming generations will be paying for those who will be drawing a pension at the age of 65.
For the information of the house I may say that the other day when I went to western Canada, more specifically to Winnipeg, I read this article in the Winnipeg Tribune of February 25, 1965:

Anyone who was naive enough to hope that the Canada pension plan would end political bidding in old age security must feel sadly disappointed. Political parties and individual M.P.'s have responded to the scheme by initiating an auction for votes worse than anything in the last quarter of a century.

At this point I would say that when claims are made they do not always come from members of parliament, as shown by this letter received from the senior women's committee for pension increases, 172 Madison avenue, Toronto 5, Ontario. I shall read that letter in a few moments. I think that all the members must have received a similar letter. The article continues:

There are calls for blanket increases in amounts of pensions and for introduction of new categories of beneficiaries from all sides of the house. The result is that the plan is now a hopeless mixture of political insurance and political welfare.
The bidding can have very serious effects in the future because of the vast sums of money involved.

This is what it means: $5 billion in round figures. The government says it will need $5, $7 or perhaps $10 billion within the next ten years. Well, we shall definitely not accept Bill No. C-136.
It is obvious that the government proposes to withhold even more from the pay cheques or the income of Canadian citizens, when we are not even able to dispose of our national production. Why does the government not use funds available at the Bank of Canada, according to the actual production in Canada, and instead of calling this a pension plan, while it is really a form of taxation, it could replace it by a national dividend based on Canadian production, on the actual resources of the country, and not on debts, on the poverty of the Canadian people, but rather 20220-804}
Canada Pension Plan
on the existing abundance and on our potential production.
That is what the government does not want to consider. Instead of cutting into the financial system, a new tax is invented, in short national or provincial "barbottes"; whatever you call it, it is still confiscating small salaries and national revenue.
Mr. Chairman, in 1964 the national production amounted to $46 billion. In 1965, it will probably reach $48, $49 or $50 billion. In 1964, the total national revenue was about $33 billion. Therefore, there exists a discrepancy of $13 billion between production and purchasing power in the hands of consumers. And we do not have to call this social credit in order to understand and to realize that everybody knows about it. Stores abound in products of all kinds. Everybody knows that industrial warehouses are filled to capacity. We do not know what to do with Canadian production.
One can also realize that salaries are not sufficient to buy the goods produced. Look at the situation of wage earners throughout Canada.
They have mortgaged their income for three, four and five years in order to buy this year's production. They have bought a refrigerator, a car on finance, they have borrowed from Household Finance or any other finance company. Why? Because salaries are insufficient, the total national revenue is insufficient to purchase the production.
There are still economists who contend that salaries will eventually be able to buy the production in this country. Mr. Chairman, I see two economists before me, the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Pepin) and the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean (Mr. Lamontagne), people who do not yet believe in the theories of social credit but who do not suggest any remedy to the government. It was expected that as members of the federal cabinet they would work miracles, but the only solution they put forward amounts to a tax increase; this will bring about a decrease instead of an increase in the distribution of production since the purchasing power will have been confiscated. Such is their logic and that is what we are fighting, not only in this house but outside as well.
When we preached the theory of Major C. H. Douglas, the theorem of A + B, the economists used to say that it was basically wrong. What does this theorem say? That salaries must be at a level allowing the production to be purchased. That is true; it is an

Canada Pension Plan
established fact. Today, we have the evidence before us; it is clear that the production will be bought, but it will be renewed year after year at a quicker pace than the increase in salaries, because at the rate we are going, there will always be a surplus of production over purchasing power, which is the income in the hands of consumers.
Economists contend that salaries will be adequate to buy the production. It is like saying that any person who is born will die some day; why worry, for in the end the death total will equal the birth total and consequently, there will be no increase in population at any time, because in the end, the total of deaths will be equivalent to the total of births. A very intelligent statement, indeed. Only it must be remembered that some people die at 70, 55, 40, 35, 12, and even infants die. Thus, the time element must be taken into account, because at a certain time every year, there is an increase in the population of Canada as in all the countries of the world. It is absurd to claim that there will be no more problems because in the end, everybody dies.
With regard to national production, it is exactly the same thing, because we produce more than we earn, and the government, instead of making up for the lack of money and credit, presents bills which reduce the consumers' purchasing power.
We noticed yesterday in the blue book of estimates for 1965-that the interest on the public debt-and this is only one item- amounts to $1,103 million. That is sacred.
Why not cut into that? Do you know that $1,103 million represents $55 per capita in Canada, if you assume that the population totals 20 million people; $55 per capita, $550 for a family of 10 people, $275 for a family of five people. That is what it means. Why does the government not cut into those interests, instead of taking from the pockets and wallets of the people who build Canada?
I am not indulging in partisan politics either Grit, Tory or what have you, I do not care. Let us deal with the problems and look for the solution where it might be available.
The pension plan is no solution because with such standards it means additional taxation, and the Canadian people are fed up with taxes.
Did the Canadian people ask for such a plan? I have just visited the universities all across Canada, from British Columbia to the maritime provinces, and everywhere in those universities I have met people, young and
[Mr. Caouette.l
old, and they do not want that pension plan because they do not want to pay more taxes.
The government, the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of National Health and Welfare claim that it is a good thing for the economic development in Canada, as was said a while ago by a government member. We have private organizations, private enterprises, that can provide pension plans for those who want them without any obligation, without coercion, without any strait-jacket. This pension plan is a strait-jacket that is forced on everybody.
We read in the clause concerning contributions that the employer will pay his share, that he shall collect from the employee and hand the contributions over to the government under penalty of mortal sin; he shall hand them over under penalty of a fine of retaliation from the government.
What does the government pay the employer for that work? Employers are forced to do the same thing as regards income tax. The Minister of National Revenue does that, but what does he do to have the employer do the work for the government? Absolutely nothing; but the employer is severely penalized if he does not act according to the government's requirement. Is that not dictatorship? Is it not a direct violation of the freedom of enterprise?

There is no more need for those people. They are too old. And the pension plan will come into force only in 1970, that is five years hence, for those having reached the age of 65.
Why not grant a pension which would allow the older people to live decently, why not give them more than they get at the present time, and without further increasing taxes?
Mr. Chairman, there is not enough credit in circulation; the point is not so much to
increase taxes as to distribute dividends. The result would be different. Some find this funny. It may be, but do you not think it funny to have a system like this where you have to resort to devious means in order to find money? They call it economic growth, whereas it is really economic depression, since some purchasing power is taken away from the consumers.
Mr. Chairman, we object to this pension plan. We shall vote against it, and we wish to advise the citizens of the province of Quebec not to be trapped by their provincial government, which intends to establish a pension scheme complying in all respects with the standards of the federal scheme we have been studying.
We want the government to start dealing with the real problem. That problem is due not to a lack of goodwill on the part of the Canadian people, but to a lack of will on the part of the government. It is a fact that the government does not want to touch the present financial system. You can go after the Canadian people or anybody else, but keep away from the financial system. That is something sacred. Leave that system alone, but go after all Canadian citizens. Let us go and tax the employer, the employee, all classes of society, let us take away from them

all we can of what they own, while doing our utmost to respect and keep adoring the golden calf as we have been doing so well since confederation.
Mr. Chairman, we do not expect to perform miracles and we are not asking for any. However, we do ask the government to take its responsibilities and start putting the financial system in step with realities in Canada, instead of putting Canadians in step with poverty.
The government should put Canadians in step with this land of plenty, help them to benefit from the wealth of goods Canada can produce at present. In order to do this, the government must absolutely have the will and determination to cut into the present financial system to free the private individual in Canada, in short, to liberate the whole Canadian people.
