Mr. Chairman, I thought that since this matter had been raised-the minister brought it up herself-we are entitled to give explanations on clause 1 of the bill. It seems to me that the restricted circle of committee members is not the only one which has the right to know and to disguise; we are also entitled to explanations concerning the various steps taken. In my opinion, it is a personal prerogative, Mr. Chairman.
We are now considering socialist and communist-inspired legislation of the worst kind, one that only the Liberal party, with the assistance of the N.D.P., could have introduced.
It is hypocritical legislation because under the pretence of providing protection for Canadian citizens, the government is levying a new tax that 90 per cent of the people cannot afford to pay. What will a person get at the age of 65? One hundred and four dollars, $52, $40 or $35 depending on his earning power. Average workers will be taxed throughout their lives to get back only 10 per cent of the money they contributed.
Hypocritical legislation because the government fails to tell the people that in 10 years time, it will have collected $6,000 to $7,000
[The Chairman.]

million from them without giving them back a single cent.
Hypocritical legislation because employers will always have to pay 50 per cent of their employees' contributions without ever getting a return on their money.
Hypocritical legislation because the poor labourer will again have to pay a tax on his gross income without having a word to say about it and because he may have to submit report after report to get a refund 12 to 18 months late.
Hypocritical legislation indeed, because neither employers nor contributors are being told that they will have to submit to three examinations, those of the federal and provincial income tax officers and that of the officials who will look after the insurance premiums of this socialist federal scheme.
Mr. Chairman, I say it is a socialist measure because it does, in fact, nationalize the savings of the average worker; it is the conscription of savings in Canada. The citizen is no longer a human being; he becomes a mere number.
It is with such a system that the communists succeeded in taking over a third of the world. The best proof that we have gone a long way in that direction is that, if someone tries to fight that dictatorship, he is shown the door.
Mr. Chairman, I have here evidence that will show to the house that this pension plan is insuring people who are already insured. Nobody took the trouble to wonder if the people who could not contribute to a private pension plan should not be the first considered by the government. Of course not, Mr. Chairman. What happens? The workers already insured by private insurance plans are covered by that plan.
Senator Croll asked a question about the people who are insured in Canada. The answer is found on page 14:
Trust funds	1,261,382
Group life Insurance annuities in Canada	560,539
Federal government group annuities 155,586
As we can see, Mr. Chairman, about 50 per cent of the labour force today contribute to private insurance plans. But it is precisely on that group of people that the federal government wants to impose a pension plan which will prevent them in the future from contributing to a private plan, since the working man cannot afford to pay two insurance premiums.
Mr. Chairman, I have here further evidence from a company which appeared before the committee. I mention it to show that there
Canada Pension Plan
was some opposition shown in the committee, but that it was not taken very seriously.
This company states that, since 1938, it has operated a contributory pension plan for its employees, which was amended from time to time and, at present, the company expects to pay to the employees and their widows, pensions of a higher level than those generally prevailing in our Canadian industry. The company in question would prefer to maintain its plan without changing it, but it admits the impossibility to do so because of the establishment of a public contributory pension plan such as proposed by Bill No. C-136.
That is why I was telling you a moment ago that the pension plan we are considering at this time is nothing more than the taking over of private plans and the end of such plans.
I will read the evidence of a company's representative who presented his views before the committee.
We believe that the financing of the benefits provided for in Bill No. C-136 will deceive the public and probably be misinterpretated by the legislators.
Another witness stated the following concerning taxation:
Herewith is a clipping of the Globe and Mail issue of February 2, 1965. Therein is stated what I believe will be the opinion of the ordinary Canadian citizen when he realizes the nature of the Canada pension plan. The purpose of the "conversation" is to point out how illogical it is to collect a tax on salaries throughout the country and then to give part of it to some senior citizens but not to others, while reserving a large portion of it.
I wanted to mention this to the Minister of National Revenue who argued in the discussion of the previous clauses, that the government was not imposing a tax.
But the best testimony I can submit is that of Mr. Douglas R. Butt, as reported on page 2030 of the proceedings outlining the needs of a pension plan.
Normally, in the presentation of any program, whether to the public, or to others affected by the program, one of the first things dealt with is its need. In the case of the Canada pension plan, there has been no such demonstration.
And further on, he goes on to say:
The proposed Canada pension plan falls in the second category. To assume that a large portion of future retired employees will need help simply because the present generation needs help would be policy.
Then, Mr. Douglas R. Butt put several very interesting questions. First, he asks:
Has it been determined, with a reasonable degree of confidence, that our retirement problem is not a temporary one, caused partly by the depression.

Canada Pension Plan
partly by inflation, partly by the absence of pension plans in the past?
Has it been determined that the needs for government assistance in pensions for many future generations will be sufficiently widespread to make an overall irreversible compulsory plan desirable?
Have studies been made projecting various employees savings capacities of the future years, to determine how much pension they can provide on their own?
And here is another question put by Mr. Douglas R. Butt:
Why has it been considered necessary to combine the death and disability benefits, which are in the nature of catastrophe insurance, with retirement benefits, the amounts of which are interrelated?
I think such questions should have prompted the committee to study the matter thoroughly. If the committee had done so, I am sure it would not have reached such a unanimous decision.
Here is a fourth question put by Mr. Douglas R. Butt:
Why have employees direct and indirect taxes for O.A.S. benefits been so zealously ignored when discussing the cost of the proposed Canada pension plan?
And the administration cost of this famous plan, again according to the minister's estimates, will be between $17 and $18 million, when the existing old age security plan is only costing $2 million in that respect.
Speaking about the economic results he puts this question:
Has any consideration been given to analysis of the effects of the plan upon the average man's capacity to save, rather than upon the average amount of savings?
I think the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) dealt fully with the effect it will have on the economic expansion which Liberal members boasted about, while all it will do will be to take away from the consumers what purchasing power they had.
And now, a sixth question from Mr. D. R. Butt:
If, in fact, future incomes are to grow and capacity to save is to increase, why do we need a compulsory government sponsored pension plan?
And the seventh question:
Has serious consideration been given to the possible harmful effect of allowing the provincial governments unrestricted use of the plan funds?
All this goes to show, Mr. Chairman, that some submissions were surely against the Canada pension plan.
I did not have time to peruse all the proceedings and I would have needed to read every page of it in order to convince the committee of the whole, which has certainly not been convinced by the minister, that this

pension plan is not what should have been provided by this government.
When I see how some actuaries have been treated, I am dumbfounded. To think that an actuary who dared utter a word of reason was immediately dismissed, that he lost his job because he accused the government of using this scheme to build up a substantial fund. And he even charged the government with false representations.
In this pension plan why not resort to a referendum? On the contrary everything was rushed through while the house was not in session. The thing has been disguised and those who could best inform the people are not allowed to express their views.
I say that Mr. John Kroeker is absolutely right, and that the government used the most unseeming and dictatorial means, not to say the most communistic, in order to impose the second veiled report, in other words, the second income tax upon the Canadian people.
We are compelled to participate in the most sinister national operation, while telling the people that it is being conducted for its security. The people are being exploited and told that it is for their own good. No member from the two old line parties protested against such an encroachment upon human liberty. They are conniving to further fetter the people with new taxes.
When will this end? Where will those hypocritical methods lead us but to communism, because communism means the absolute control of the state. And you, gentlemen of the government, are on the very path leading to it; keep on giving numbers to the people, sending them to work where it pleases you, in order to better control their salaries and restrain their freedom of speech as you did recently.
Tomorrow their will be a single party, you will present to people only one candidate in your so-called popular elections, and you will call it the social democrat party, as if to besmirch for the last time the word democracy.
We are in favour of a pension plan, of the one we now have. Let us increase the benefits to $100 per month, if need be, at age 65.
We are in favour of a second plan, yes, but provided contributions are paid on a voluntary basis.
Mr. Chairman, we have already accepted a compulsory pension plan for which we are now paying out of our taxes. We believed, and we still believe, that it was necessary for the protection of our old people and

that, not only for some of them, but especially for the poorest throughout the country. We paid our contributions because we had no alternative, but when it comes to a second plan, also compulsory, and I would even say a third plan, since we now contribute for social assistance and sickness assistance, well we protest.
Mr. Chairman, I think it would have been much more sensible for the committee to present such a plan on a voluntary basis because it would then have been accepted by the house. Moreover, it could have competed with the hundreds of private insurance plans now being offered on the market. It could probably have favourably compared with those private plans and have been an incentive and even have set a standard. When one plans to purchase insurance, one always wonders how much it will cost. Now, as regards this pension plan, I wonder what it will cost. We wonder what it will cost the Canadian citizens. To find out, I did some figuring last night. I took the case of an 18 year old man, a farmer, since my region is 95 per cent rural, and I noted that he will have to pay $158.40 annually.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, just before supper we were listening to a member of the Creditiste party. Most of what he had to say had that old familar ring which one who has lived under Social Credit in Alberta in the last 30 years finds all to familiar- the terror of the big businessman, the ogre of taxes, and the wonder at what they can relieve us from. However, no matter how much of what he said deserves to be overlooked as kindly as we can, now and then, being a true disciple of the Social Crediters, he tied in a little bit of common sense, a little bit of criticism here and there of certain matters before applying the magic ointment. Certainly he cannot be criticized for reminding us that this pension plan is going to have a tremendous impact on the country, and I think that this is the time to take a sober second look and ask ourselves whether we really need it. This is the time to ask ourselves how much we need it, before embarking upon the implementation of the plan in its present form.
For one thing, this plan is compulsory. There must on all sides of the house, I think, be the feeling that if a plan is to be compulsory it must be shown beyond any shadow of doubt that the amount of good it is going to do outweighs not just any possible disadvantages or harm it may do, or overshadows any weakness in the plan itself, but that it is so necessary, so essential, that it is going to do so much good for so many people

in the country, that it justifies this democratic nation of ours in taking the step, which many of us find so dreadful, of saying to the people that they must comply in this regard with the will of the government.
There are many people, Mr. Chairman, who have given the country the impression that this debate has dragged on for too long. I for one can hardly understand the attitude of some members of the press, who feel that we should have flitted from paragraph to paragraph of this bill with hardly another look at it. I do not think we could justify ourselves as members of this House of Commons, in view of the tremendous effect that this bill will have upon the country in general, if we hesitated in taking a little while to pause and reflect, to search and search again, and if necessary to retrace our steps in order to see how far we must go to achieve our objective, how well we can achieve it in this particular fashion, and whether there is some other way to achieve it.
I for one have grave misgivings about the plan generally. Certainly I have always advocated, as have most members in this house, that we should have a Canada pension plan. We know there are many working people in this country who, because of the nature of their employment, the transitory jobs they hold, or perhaps because of the particular pay scale they are on, have not found it possible, or in their opinion desirable, to participate in a private plan. For these people we have all wanted to provide something. We have wanted to provide a framework as a result of which those who want a little more security for their old age may find something to cling to. I think the desire for this is Canada wide. It is found and reflected not just in those who need the legislation we are trying to implement, but in the vast majority of citizens who feel so compassionately the needs of their fellow citizens who are not so fortunate. I want to emphasize that this feeling is Canada wide.
I am not sure whether my reticence in connection with this plan is based mainly on this one point, but certainly it does have a tremendous influence upon the way I look at this bill. To me a plan for Canadians should be for all Canadians. If a plan is good enough for a man in Newfoundland or Alberta or British Columbia or Ontario, it should be good enough for the rest of the provinces. The first objection I have, then, to the present plan is the fact that it does not apply to the province of Quebec.

1 can understand very well much of the reasoning of those in that province who say they prefer their own plan. I can understand that they believe their plan is better, and it may be that in certain aspects it is better. But none of this convinces me that in this country it is not possible to enact legislation of such a far reaching character that it will not be substantially acceptable to all people in the country, that it will not substantially meet the same needs, and satisfy the same desires and visions of people in all parts of the land. If I am correct in this, then I suggest it is simply a matter of making sure that the federal government gets together with the provinces and irons out the differences with a little give and take here and there, to the end that we have just one plan.
I am sure all of us in this house who had something to say on portability, or who read about it, must be disturbed by the thought that this pension plan cannot be called truly portable. It is possible to have minor changes by variations in the plan. Certainly the plan in respect of the province of Quebec will vary somewhat from the Canada pension plan. However, I must remind hon. members that each province has the same rights as the province of Quebec and may decide to withdraw or opt out and set up different plans at some future date. Perhaps the province of Alberta will decide to do so, two or three years after the adoption of this plan, and four or five years later perhaps the province of Manitoba will opt out. We do not really know what will happen, but the fact is that we are leaving this important possibility open.
There is a degree of portability to this plan, although not the degree we had hoped would exist. I suggest that a great deal of the agitation created by the proposal of this Canada pension plan relates to the fact that a great number of people are already participants in pension plans which for obvious reasons will not be portable. A great many workmen in this country are chained to their jobs because they have paid toward pension plans over a long period of time and must stay another ten or 15 years in order to reap the full benefit. In many cases perhaps they would not reap any benefit at all from their past contributions if they were to leave now and become participants in the plan now before us for consideration.
This aspect of portability is a very important one to a very large number of people. We have not as yet implemented this plan, but we have already realized that one province feels its own plan is a better plan. I
Canada Pension Plan
am sure that after we have gained some experience in the pension field, and after the province of Quebec has gained some experience, we will all know which aspects of which plans are the most advantageous, at which time perhaps other provinces will opt out, establishing their own pension plans based on these most advantageous aspects. If that should happen, I suggest we will no longer have the portability in respect of pension plans administered by the federal government and the various opted out provinces.

Mr. Chairman, I hear the parliamentary secretary say "come, come". I wish I had the optimism he has. I am sure he was as confident in the first plan which his minister introduced in this house as he is in this one. I can see him yet applauding his minister when she said: This is the Canada pension plan and we will adopt it or I will not be here. I remember that hon. gentleman thumping his desk enthusiastically, in the same way as he now says "come, come".
Perhaps wisdom will accompany experience, but perhaps it will not. In any event I think we are now considering what is formally called the third pension plan, and informally referred to as the umpteenth plan. I should think the parliamentary secretary might have learned a little discretion.
My remarks to this point have been directed toward the one all-Canadian aspect of the Canada pension plan that has given me difficulty. I feel that what is good enough for one Canadian is good enough for all Canadians. Having mentioned that one point which has bothered me in respect of this pension plan, relating to portability, and which I am afraid we can no longer hope for, I should deal with another unsatisfactory facet.
While there is a certain compulsory requirement embodied in this plan, we must relate it to the people who will be mainly affected, namely those Canadians who are not in the high income brackets. In this regard, what we are doing is suggesting that it is our considered judgment these people should pay a certain percentage of their incomes toward investment in retirement benefits. Many of these people already contribute to private pension plans. Many of them have indicated to me that with the rising cost of living, in conjunction with other factors, they are interested in how much

Canada Pension Plan
cash they have in their pockets, because this determines how they live. They may well be getting wiser in respect of savings investments, and we hope that the workingman is becoming wiser and more educated as to the advantages attending income separate from wages, but we must realize that these same people are finding it much more difficult to put aside a portion of their incomes for the future. One has only to look at the amount of consumer credit now being used in this country to realize that most people in this income bracket are living beyond their incomes. They are using their credit to live today with the hope that they will be able to pay tomorrow. The last thing they want is for someone to come along and take cash out of their pockets in order to look after their retirement 20 years from now. This cash in their pockets is now paying the bills they incurred two years ago.
We all agree, I am sure, that the attitude adopted by these people at this time is a shortsighted one, and one which the wise, prudent and careful family man would not follow. These individuals should be putting aside something to look after their retirement years; but that is only a theoretical approach to the problem. What is happening in this country today in respect of the workingman is that he is living from day to day on his income. This is the habit he has adopted; and he is looking, perhaps, to the government to look after his retirement years.
I think we must face this situation realistically when we suggest that this pension plan will place all individuals at retirement in security and comfort. We must seriously consider the suggestion that this pension plan will do those things, and therefore is the thing which should be provided for the people because they are not wise enough to provide for themselves. It may well be that this is a proper action to take in the best interests of the people, but unless we convince these people of that fact, we are going to incur great difficulty.
Most of the individuals I have had the opportunity of speaking with in respect of this pension plan have been most vocal in their opposition to it. I have certain misgivings about the plan because it is not a truly Canadian pension plan and not truly portable, but perhaps I have less misgivings than those people with whom I have spoken. On the other hand, perhaps I have given them too sympathetic an ear. However, I belong to the old school which believes that we should be very careful in telling people what is best

for them. I feel we should be very careful when we attempt to force people to come into a scheme of any kind because we believe it is the best scheme for them. Surely now is the time, before we have gone any further, to take another look at this proposition.
I am afraid in reply the minister will say that many people resent this plan because they do not understand it and do not appreciate its advantages. Perhaps she will suggest that these people do not realize its importance. If that is the case, then we have failed in another duty: We have failed to inform the people as to exactly what this plan will do.
I am well aware that the Conservative party is not in a position to point a finger at the Liberals and suggest that their propaganda is not as effective as it should be, because we have learned to our sorrow that Liberal propaganda is ten times more effective than ours. They are much better salesmen than we are, and are able to sell their lies ten times as fast as we can sell the truth. However, in respect of this plan, which is supposedly designed to benefit the public rather than the Liberal party, I am afraid the Liberal party has not displayed any great selling potentiality.

Mr. Chairman, our discussions on the Canada pension plan, Bill No C-136, have now reached a fairly advanced stage. I have heard several proposals and amendments concerning the pension plan, but I must say right now that the scheme does not provide assistance for the most needy; it does not fill the needs of the Canadian people.
It will mostly enable the government to accumulate capital; it will also be a compulsory levy against the income of the small wage earners and yet, it will exempt those who earn over $5,000. It will discriminate against the poor and those in the low income bracket.
Mr. Chairman, the scale of contributions- if I may express myself that way-provides
Canada Pension Plan
for a levy of 1.8 per cent on earnings of $600 to $5,000, 0.9 per cent for incomes up to $10,000, 0.4 per cent up to $20,000 and 0.2 per cent up to $40,000. Therefore the contribution is not national in scope, but discriminatory. The benefits are also very different. They range from $3 for a 45 year old widow to $104 for a 70 year old widower. Regional, nowhere. National, nowhere, except on the capitalization for the nation of about $8 billion for the next 10 years.
All this is not yet voted and should not be voted as drafted and submitted. What we should have is a flat rate, pay as you go. Equal taxation for all, identical rates at all levels, and for all incomes. This preamble is not pure phraseology, because I would want very much to point out that in present circumstances, it is not the future of Canada or of Canadians that is at stake; it is rather the future of great institutions which is at stake in a prosperous Canada. The fate that is at issue today is that of the human being in the family, in the home, in the residence, in the abode where all of the 19,400,000 Canadian citizens live physically and spiritually, each of them as a total and unique person.
Canada must be prosperous at the level of the human being and the family. That is the point to which you must give your complete adhesion. If I could secure such adhesion from each one of you today, the conditions of misery, insecurity and poverty would be solved, and each human being, each Canadian family would find joy in living with economic freedom and personal, temporal, intellectual and spiritual security.
Canada exists at the level of the human being and the family. That is where Canada has real and concrete life. At the level of provinces, municipalities, large institutions, universities, big companies, stock exchanges, banks and co-operatives, at the level of intermediate bodies, pressure groups and associations of all kinds, Canada is not at the level of life, but at the level of administration.
The administration takes care of itself first. "Charity begins at home". And I accept that. It is in order. But if charity begins at home, it does not end there. It must go further, go to the end of its work and reach the human person, the family, its ultimate reason for existing.
And here I invite not only the 265 members of this house, the 26 ministers of the government, not only honourable senators, but also all the managers and presidents of our big institutions, all those in charge of big private

Canada Pension Plan
and public bodies, all the university graduates in all fields, all those whom it is customary to call the elite of society, I invite them all to complete and to improve the proposal under consideration, Bill No. C-136, the Canada pension plan.
This is the last chance. What will be done with the plan will determine once and for all whether Canada will continue to be run as it was in the past or whether it has decided to keep pace with modern administration, as it has kept abreast of modern production and automation. Are we going to keep on impoverishing the people to enrich the wealthy through our administrative monetary, economic and political measures? Or are we finally going to realize that we must definitely restore the balance between individuals, families and institutions, between income expenditures and surpluses, between taxes and profits? The restoration of balance or the continuation of chaos, that is the choice we have.
We must seek to solve existing problems instead of creating new ones. We refuse to raise our children in a world of hate, corruption and injustice, like the one in which we live and which is being set up by Bill No. C-136.
Mr. Chairman, the "income-expense-profit" formula acknowledged by all prominent economists, accountants, engineers, actuaries and administrators at the head of all great institutions should be made possible at all levels of administration in Canada and, first of all, at the level of the human being and the family, its natural environment.
If every human being, in every Canadian family, can manage his affairs properly according to the "income-expense-profit" formula, there is no need to worry about institutions which can administer themselves as administration and production agents above individuals and families.
Individuals, families and institutions, this sums up the five speeches I delivered in this house and which appear in the official report.
I delivered one on August 20, 1964, another on September 10, another on October 28 and 29, another on November 17, another on December 17, and on February 25, 1965.

Canada Pension Plan
I was saying, for instance, that very few listened to the speeches I have made here. In any case, I did my duty as a citizen in making those speeches in the house.
Mr. Chairman, I have attempted to table papers which have been refused by the joint committee set up to consider Bill No. C-136. That was their business, but I have explained my viewpoint and I have done my duty as a member according to my conscience and my conviction.
Mr. Chairman, we have no right to let people rot in poverty, in insecurity, in want, while we have here salaries of $18,000, $25,000 and $40,000. We have no right to let families go without the necessities of life in Canada, a prosperous country, so prosperous that just in the year 1963-64, the shares of the 800 biggest companies on the Montreal stock exchange increased from $44 billion to $77 billion, that is an increase of 75 per cent or $33 billion in two years. And that is what we call austerity years for the people of Canada.
Concerning Bill No. C-136, I am bringing official evidence where you are requested to improve, complete and perfect your Canada pension plan. I am not the only one to express this opinion, but I am also offering an alternative. You refuse to hear me. Could you listen to any others?
You were accused before the joint committee, by the Canadian chamber of commerce, of allocating the greatest part of the benefits to the Canadians who do not need them and neglecting those who have no means of support whatsoever. Did I not say so in the speech I made in this house on November 17, 1964?
When the	association	of	life	insurerscharges you with extending your system of contributions and capitalization over the years to come, with imposing rates ranging from 3.6 per cent to 5 per cent in a few years, and accumulating a huge capital instead of seeing to welfare under the pay as you go system, from year to year, did I not tell you the	same thing	in	the	speech Idelivered on	October 28-29,	1964,	when Iexplained the philosophy	of	the	"personal
vital right" as a right which our government owes to every human being in Canada, and which is payable out of our annual resources which are quite sufficient for that purpose?

Canada Pension Plan
from young people-the philosophy of the personal vital right shows clearly that every human being in Canada should receive, out of the annual production and without personal costs, the minimum which he is already guaranteed under our Canadian laws, namely chapter 44 of 1960 statutes of Canada. You will see this in the speech I made on September 10, 1964.
When another actuary and notary, Mr. J. W. Joyce, president of the committee on social security of the Canadian association of actuaries, warns you that the Canada pension plan contains within itself all the possible sources of dissatisfaction and will give rise to many difficulties in coming years; when the powerful Canadian manufacturers association suggests that the pension plan should be revised and managed on a pay as you go basis annually, that the whole plan should be rejected and replaced by a flat-rate plan, as an extension of the existing old age pension plan, do you not think that I am pleased, since I expressed exactly the same points of view in the explanation of the right of all and every one?
When the brief of the province of Ontario suggests recommendations that the Minister of National Health and Welfare herself, the sponsor of Bill No. C-136, appreciates so much that she says: "Ontario would have acted wisely in making its suggestions known earlier". Why not do it? But why such a hurry? There is still time. Advantage can still be taken of those important changes suggested by Ontario.
When the social workers association blames the Canada pension plan for not taking into account those who have marginal or very low salaries or revenues, and those who do not have a regular job, while the vital right plan of all and everyone avoids all those disadvantages, what is done of a single plan?
When the joint board of directors of the chambers of commerce of Ontario and Quebec say that the plans proposed by the province of Quebec and the whole of Canada would not help needy people, would pay bonuses where there is no need and completely ignore 1J million Canadians 65 years and over, li million of them having a submarginal standard of living, what is thought?

[Mr. Latulippe.l

Eddy Co. in Hull across the Ottawa river behind the parliament buildings, clearly indicates that this pension plan of the government, if it is ever implemented, will increase production costs and weaken even more our competitive position on the export markets, why not do something about it?

When the 84 page actuarial report distributed to hon. members on March 6 and in November 1964 had no signature and was not read completely by any hon. member or any minister as far as I know, because it is too learnedly incomprehensible and for a very good reason because it can be seen on the second page of that unsigned report: "A definition is given later on of four expressions concerning the earnings of contributors which will be frequently used in the report". Where? And what should we think?
It must be pointed out that those expressions are only applicable for the purpose of the report. They were chosen so that they would need as little explanation as possible. Let us get the pith and marrow of that preliminary precaution.
When all happens in this way, when the Canadian labour council, itself in favour of the project, recommends very important reforms and amendments to the whole thing, we see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) in the house and outside, attempt by every possible means to press for the adoption of the project, against every opinion, to have it passed as fast as possible, bending over backwards to undertake the necessary corrections as fast as possible in due time and according to government policy.
We are against any collective plan which incorporates people against their will as the Pearson-Lesage plan.

Third, we are against such methods of financing decent pensions to old people, that is financing pensions through taxes or compulsory contributions deducted at the source.
In the fourth place, we object to that method because it enables the state to gain control of individuals' savings and dispose of them as it wishes, and finally leads to a state control over the whole economy.
Our movement believes that private savings should not be invested in uneconomic public projects.
The construction of bridges, roads, schools, sidewalks and all uneconomic services should not be financed through "freezing" private savings, but rather through new credits, created by the central bank according to the needs and made available to the persons concerned; those new credits should be loaned without interest and refundable over long periods: such is the theory which the Creditistes have always upheld. They establish a difference between private capital intended to develop economic concerns, and uneconomic works, the latter to be financed through social capital.
The Creditistes believe that pensions should be considerably increased and exceed $100 a month at age 60 or 65.
None of the pensioners receive enough at the present time. I have in my riding old people who ask for higher pensions, they say they do not have enough. What is required by their health condition? A healthy housing, diversified leisure adapted to their age. That is the only thing which is claimed to give them satisfaction. Old people complain that they do not have enough. According to their household budget, it costs them $200, $300 or $400 a month to live, and yet they receive only $75. In a country such as this, we cannot reach the goal we set ourselves and help the people by the injection of compulsory pensions plans.
What does prevent our senior citizens from enjoying full security in their old age? It is the present financial system which nobody wants to disturb. Whereas things, physical realities would permit older people to end their life peacefully, the financial system is opposed to that because it is not adjusted and does not allow distribution of goods at the same rate as their production.
Should the pension plan be contributory? Social Credit says no. Failing rational methods, or financing such as the one suggested by the Social Credit, we in this corner of the house prefer that government pensions be paid by way of income taxes-

ten years, that is from the age of 65 to 70 or nine years after the death of her husband. Another advantage of pension plans sponsored by private insurance companies is that they are prepared by businessmen and not by pickpockets.

I endeavoured to point out to them that the Canada pension plan will in no way affect the pension plan to which they now belong. I am just trying to say before continuing with my remarks that the people of Canada do not know all about the plan. Regardless of

how much talk has gone on in the house, I find that there is a great misunderstanding of the plan throughout the country.
I have made a few notes. For instance, many people think that everyone is going to get $104 a month on retirement. After discussing the plan we know that this is not the case; but the fact is that many of the people I have talked to have said, "This must be a wonderful thing, because when I reach 65 years of age I am going to get $104 a month". The people of Canada do not know these things. I will come to old age security in a moment, because that is one of the things to which I want to refer. Many people are wondering what is going to happen to their present contributory plans and we feel that the discussion we have had in the house should have enlightened everyone in Canada. I am sorry to say it has not. I have found this to be so in the case of most of the people to whom I have talked who have asked these questions. Some of the people in the cities I have gone through have even come to me and said, "Is the Canada pension plan going to be compulsory? Do I have to belong to it?" The minister nods his head. I say to the minister that the people of Canada generally do not know too much about this plan. I believe, too, that the people of Canada have every reason to be very cautious of this legislation, because we must remember that there have been three other versions of the pension plan presented by this government and each and every one of them has been said by the government to be the acme of perfection. However, here we are on the fourth version.
I have talked to many of the young people in my area, people in their early twenties or approaching their twenty first year. I find that they feel in many respects this plan is going to be a yoke around their necks. The minister said before that in the next three months everyone will know about this plan. It is all very well to hear that, but the people of Canada do not know too much about the plan at the present time. It has been said on many occasions that after three and a half weeks of debate possibly we in the opposition

are taking too long on this legislation. I say again that, bearing in mind the young people of Canada, this is not the right attitude to take. Three, four or five weeks is not too long to debate legislation such as this; because after all, the young people before whom we are placing this plan are going to be paying for it for the next 45 years. Therefore I say that anyone who says three and a half, four or five weeks debating this plan is taking up too much time of the house should give a little further consideration to it.
This afternoon the hon. member for Fraser Valley, when speaking on the plan, mentioned several aspects of it. He spoke particularly about the portability of the plan; the benefits of portability which are involved in it. He spoke of the funds which would be available for the provinces. He also spoke of the job aspects in relation to this plan. He mentioned, too, one very important aspect of the plan, which was that it is another form of increased taxation. This is what I find to be the concern of the young people with whom I have talked-and not only the young people. I have found, upon making inquiries, that this aspect of increased taxation is of considerable concern not only to our young people but even to those people in their early and late forties. The young workers with whom I have spoken want no part of this plan; this applies to practically all of those with whom I have spoken. This may be understandable to many of us, because we know that in the early years, particularly the early years of married life, people who are living on fairly low wages feel that there are other far more important things to be putting their money into than a retirement pension.
As I say, Mr. Chairman, I have found that most of the young people say, "We do not want this plan. We do not feel that the government should make it compulsory for us to join it". Then you talk to people in their early and mid-fifties. The wage earners in this group, I must admit, generally have a different outlook; they can see they are going to get a windfall. This applies to most of the people in the age group 53 to 58, and therefore this plan is quite acceptable to them. But let us take a look at how this plan affects a great many younger workers. I am speaking of people with whom I have talked and who have pointed these things out to me. There is the case of a young worker who already belongs to an industrial contributory pension plan. He pays 3 per cent of his wages to the company plan, and he told me that by the time he is 65 years of
Canada Pension Plan
age, if he continues with this plan he will build for himself a pension of $250 a month. He pays 4 per cent to old age security throughout his working years, and he says that is going to bring him in another $75 at age 65, under the present payments. He hopes that by the time he is 65 this allowance will have increased. Now he will have to pay another 1.8 per cent to the Canada pension plan, which if he makes $5,000 a year in his last ten working years will qualify him for another $104 a month. He says this will bring him in a pension of $429 a month, which is a lot more money than he is making at the present time. This is the way people look at it; they look at what they are making at the present time and what the plan is costing them.

If she is relatively the

Canada Pension Plan
same age as the husband they have figured it out this way, that by the time both reach 65 and the husband has continued in his present employment he will be entitled to $250 a month company pension, $75 a month old age security and $104 a month Canada pension plan, whereas his wile will be entitled to $75 a month old age security, and possibly $104 a month Canada pension plan, and approximately $75 to $85 a month from her contributory pension plan. This works out at a total pension of approximately $685 a month for the two of them.
Some people might say this is all well and good, but the trouble with the young worker is that he is paying for all this throughout the years when his expenses are the greatest. It has been pointed out to me that in many cases people will have a bigger income when they retire than they made throughout their working years.
These are just some of the reasons why I say there are many aspects of this plan about which we should be cautious. Despite the fact that in general I am in favour of contributory pension plans, I feel the government could have produced a much more desirable plan, a plan that would be much more acceptable to the Canadian people.
I do not know whether it has been brought to the minister's attention that a person making $20,000 a year actually gets off much easier under the Canada pension plan than a person making $5,000 a year. When this was first brought to my attention it did not seem correct, but when you look at the figures it is quite apparent that the richer you are the less this plan costs you.
If you have $5,000 a year, a wife and two children, the cost of the plan is $79. That is the gross cost; but you get an income tax credit which leaves the net cost at $62.41. If you earn $20,000 a year the gross cost is still $79, but your tax rebate is much greater, so that instead of paying $62, as does the man with $5,000 a year, you only pay $43. The man with $5,000 a year actually pays 50 per cent more in his contributions than the man making $20,000 a year.
Though I believe it is too late now for further amendments to this bill I am quite sure that when the plan goes into effect amendments to it will quickly be necessary. I am only sorry the government did not see fit to accept some of the amendments which were proposed during discussion of the bill. The things I have mentioned tonight are matters which were brought to my attention after we had begun debating the plan in this

chamber. In conclusion, I think all of us should take a good, hard look at the plan to see how we can improve it and make it more acceptable to the Canadian people.

Mr. Chairman, before Bill No. C-136, an act to establish in Canada a comprehensive program of old age pensions, is carried, I want to tell the house that I do not object to this pension being granted at age 65, on the contrary, because then I would like to see a pension of $100 a month granted as of January 1966.
But what I do object to is the fact that we are taxing again the small wage earners already confronted with all kinds of debts and forced to work wonders in order to make both ends meet.
Taxation affects all individuals who earn $1,000 and over, and this plan, which is simply a concealed tax, will allow the government to dig into the pockets of all the taxpayers with an income of over $600. It is really a disgrace.
It is the wrong time to raise taxes when a country has so many unemployed, 7 per cent of which reside in the province of Quebec.
All the employers and employees in Canada are discouraged, because they are working for the biggest industry in our country, the government.
In the difficult times we are going through
the government should decrease taxes thus allowing the economy to pick up, but it does exactly the opposite.
This new pension plan will start a rise in the cost of living. Some say one half or 2.5, but I will state without exaggeration that it might reach 4 per cent a year. This will bring about a salary increase and a rise in the cost of production; it all follows naturally.
A gradual increase in commercial prices has some advantages compared to the many disadvantages resulting of that pension plan, but most of those advantages will be lost if inflation proves to be a reality. The rise in salaries and in the cost of consumer products will subject the cost of living to unusual pressure.
By letting the cost of living rise in this way, we will reach a point where the costs of labour and goods will be prohibitive, thereby destroying any hope of high productivity and dislocating the economy of the country.
There are some people who are already very concerned about the problem and they

are asking questions about it. They want to know when the contributions will be increased. I tell them they need not worry about it; that it will not be long; that both our good old line parties know how to go about increasing taxes.
What would happen should the fund eventually show a deficit? Things like that were not provided for and that is why I suggest that we should provide for such a possibility. These funds should never be used for election purposes. We may grant loans to municipalities and provinces but never use such money as an election fund, since it would be playing with the money of the people.
Was such a plan conceived so as to help the individual? No. It was conceived solely for the purpose of refurnishing a fund, so as to give assistance to the provinces and the municipalities, and the greatest part of this fund will be used to cover the federal government's expenditures. This pension plan is intended to bring assistance to the provinces. I say that the foreseen results, as regards the provinces and municipalities, will be serious, not only as far as their debts are concerned but their revenues also.
If this keeps up, Canadians will have to stop smoking because all their savings will be used to pay for this famous pension plan. Is it the purpose of the Minister of National Health and Welfare to trap people by another compulsory means? We are sometimes inclined to think so, since her "plan" was not a success last year.
The small wage earner, having lived in poverty all his life, will be forced, at 65 years of age, to live again in poverty while the one who lived in wealth, thanks to a fat salary, will be able to end his years in wealth. Seen at this angle, this is surely an injustice which should preferably be foreseen and avoided.
The term compulsory so often used displeases me because it deprives individual citizens of their freedom. If people were free to accept or reject the pension plan, I would be satisfied, but as it now stands it is definitely compulsory.
And that is why I say it is a new tax which the Canadian people will have to pay and which will bring in $10 billion over a ten year period.
Instead of giving the people money, credit, purchasing power in these hard times, a compulsory contribution is extorted from them. This additional contribution will affect the small businessman, the industrialist and 20220-805
Canada Pension Plan
will keep them from expanding their business. This kills personal ambition because one feels that the more one works the less one receives and, consequently, one feels that one should not work more than one has to. Indeed, the government is sponsoring means which are discouraging people to work, even the selfemployed, and even after 65 years of age.
Mr. Chairman, I shall be brief. I only wanted to say that I shall not support this plan since I consider it as another tax and that I am encouraging the people in my riding to protest against a provincial plan which will be but a reflection of the federal plan.

Mr. Chairman, since I had no opportunity to take part in the discussion on the various clauses of the bill, I intended to make up for it on clause 1. For that reason, and because of the complexity of Bill No. C-136, I should like to only touch upon the matter of the funds which this plan will provide for various government bodies.
Capital drained under the form of compulsory savings by way of this pension plan- and I hope that the Minister of National Health and Welfare will not bear a grudge with me if I happen to rise on a few occasions during the discussion of this clause; I understand her great impatience since this, her third offspring, constitutes a colossal fraud. I wonder whether she is entitled to have that thing called her third offspring because I think it is the creature of another government that is now before us.
If I remember correctly, in her statements of July 1963, she precisely denounced such an accumulation of capital which, as she put it, could become dangerous in the hands of certain governments and play against the people depending on the way they could be used.
I hope she will understand that if at times, during the debate on this bill, we did not seem to share the same views, it may be because she has considerably changed her stand since July 1963, if we compare her statements at that time with those she made in March 1964, when she brought down Bill No. C-136. That could even be called a slow and difficult period of gestation bringing forth a monster.
Since Bill No. C-136 will certainly have
economic and political implications all across the country, it is worth the trouble to take all the time needed, even if we need one extra week, in order to give proper consideration

Canada Pension Plan
to the complications to be expected in the future.
Tonight, I particularly intend to examine what kind of state capitalism or economic and political dictatorship we can expect from the implementation of Bill No. C-136. Frankly, Mr. Chairman, I am apprehensive and even the people are beginning to wonder about the economic repercussions of this plan and about the power-since the plan is mandatory-we are giving the state in the field of pension funds. And the members in this corner of the house are not the only ones to denounce and fear this increasing interference of the state.
At this stage, I should like to put on record a statement published in La Conjoncture, a publication of the Canadian chamber of commerce, in February 1965, which deals with the increasing interference of the state and refers to the words of a cabinet member, namely, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau). Here is what the publication said:
From time to time, we are cautioned against the increasing control of the state over our lives. Those warnings are usually made by private individuals and many people are inclined to disregard them. When a minister expresses his views about the power of the state, one is apt to take him more seriously.
The federal Minister of Justice said recently to a group of Toronto lawyers that the rights of Canadians are being "seriously threatened" by growing state interference and by the inability of the citizens to protect themselves. Following the wave of emancipation which swept over most of western Europe at the time of the industrial revolution, governments, stated the minister, gradually increased almost everywhere their control over the lives of citizens, to such an extent that there is some fear the dynamism of the people might be lessened.

speechtext:
wish to speak very briefly on a subject of considerable concern to the dairymen of Canada-one which is of particular concern, I know, to the dairymen of British Columbia both in the coastal area and in the interior.
It is a subject with which I have some personal acquaintance, having milked my first cow back in 1902; I still wake up at 5.30 in the morning to milk cows that are not there. Hon. members may be interested to note that the parliamentary secretary and the member for Kootenay West are both graduates of the Ontario Agricultural College. I entered in 1909 and he was bom in 1910, but I love to see these young men climbing the hay loader to fame and influence.
I am speaking this evening on behalf of a group of people who are possibly the hardest working group of people in Canada-people who work harder and for longer hours than almost any other group in the country, that is, the dairymen.
It is for that reason that I asked the following question, as reported at page 12640 of Hansard:
. .. with respect to the proposal of the federal government to establish a national dairy authority. Can the minister assure the house that any government policy established in this respect will not conflict with the provisions of the B.C. milk industry act and its regulations?
That question is trying to get something by indirect action that it is very difficult to get by direct action under certain circumstances.
I have had letters from farm organizations, but I will just take the time to read a letter which I received from the Fraser Valley milk producers association, dated March 12. I might say that I knew some of the founders of this assocation, Mr. Berry and Mr. Hill-Tout, who were also former graduates of agriculture and were very interested in building up this institution, and the producers' sponsored legislation which protects the dairy industry in B.C. This is what he said:
Dear Sir:
On February 26th the Canadian Press Issued a release on what was reported to be the proposed policy of the federal government with respect

to the establishment of a national dairy authority, and some of the terms under which it would operate. Some of these proposals are completely impractical and would be unacceptable to the dairy industry.
With reference to the Canadian Press report, the Canadian federation of agriculture and the dairy farmers of Canada issued a joint release on March 8th, a copy of which we understand was sent to all members of the House of Commons, the Canadian Press, and weekly newspapers, etc.
I would like to urge your support for the policies contained in the joint release of March 8th.
In addition, British Columbia has a very special problems which would not be compatible with some of the principles in the alleged government policy proposals. Specifically, the proposal that producers must ship to the fluid market only or to manufacturing plants only, but not both, would be in direct conflict with the provisions of the B.C. milk industry act and regulations, which in the controlled areas of the province provides for participation in both markets for qualifying producers.
I would therefore again urge your support for the preservation of the B.C. milk industry act to the end that its provisions are not superseded by any federal government action.
Thanking you for your interest in this regard, I am,
Very truly yours,
Fraser Valley milk producers' association
That is signed by Mr. J. C. Brannick, president.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, that this B.C. legislation was the result of years of effort on the part of the producers in the dairy industry, who found it an effective protection for the producers particularly of fluid milk and dairy products. So I would appreciate it very much indeed if the parliamentary secretary could give us, in the short time available, some idea of government policy, letting us have a peek into the future, as it were. And in doing so, can he assure the house that there will be no conflict between the federal government policy with respect to the dairy industry, and the B.C. milk industry act and its regulations? I will be very interested, as I am sure will other hon. members in the house, knowing the problem of the dairy producers, in hearing the parliamentary secretary's reply.

He has suggested that I might give him a little glimpse into the future. I want to express my appreciation to him for having given me a glimpse into the past, because I did not know what it was to milk a cow in 1902. So I want to thank him for having drawn very appropriate attention to my 20220-805J

SHIPPING-INQUIRY AS TO CONSTRUCTION OF MARINA
speechtext:
On the
occasion of a by-election in the riding of Laurier, on February 10, 1964, when all my opponents lost their deposits, including the son of the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette), for which once more I am grateful to the people of my constituency, one of the invited speakers, the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets), who was then minister of public works, announced, with the authorization of the Department of Transport, that a harbour station would be built in Montreal.
This news was greeted with enthusiasm by those who attended that meeting, and the next day the press applauded that statement.
On October 2, 1964, I directed a question to the then minister of public works, pointing out to him that, since the announcement nothing of a realistic nature had been done, to my knowledge, in order to expedite the implementation of the necessary and urgent project, that is a harbour station for the city of Montreal.

That same night, the hon. member for Mai-sonneuve-Rosemont gave out a press release expressing his satisfaction at the fact that the project had been supported by the national harbours board and in which he stated, among other things, as follows:
As I have already mentioned, I do not contemplate a building of gigantic proportions, but an establishment which would be practical and would have style.
The national harbour board adds that a thorough study of the matter had established that it was a useful and necessary project, from the standpoint of tourist trade as well as from the economic standpoint. This harbour station is supposed to have all the modern equipment which is necessary to make possible a very great flexibility of movements for tourists and ships, and it must take into account the present and future needs of navigation in the Montreal harbour. An article published in he Devoir of October 3, 1964, mentioned the press release issued by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont, by the president of the executive committee of the city of Montreal, Mr. Lucien Saulnier, and by the national harbours board.
Since that press release silence has again become the keynote as far as this project is concerned, and the hon. member for Maison-neuve-Rosemont has been replaced by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) as Minister of Public Works.
I have noted with pleasure that the blue books containing the main estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1966, contains a vote of $1 million for the construction of that harbour station.
At this time the authorities of this country's metropolis should be ashamed to receive tourists coming in by sea in a ramshackle, pitiful, miserable, sorry and, I dare say, disgusting shed.
In this press release the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont added:
It is now up to Montreal to choose the site.
The president of the executive committee, Mr. Lucien Saulnier, stated that he was glad to see that the government had opened negotiations with the city of Montreal concerning the important choice of a site for a harbour station in Montreal. He added that the town planning service would have a word to say about the site of the terminal and its approaches.
According to the statements made by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont and

the president of the executive committee of the city of Montreal, it would seem that this project now comes under the city of Montreal. That is why, this afternoon, I asked about the outcome of the negotiations between the government and the municipal authorities.
Naturally, I want to know whether the town planning commission has finally reached a decision on the site of the harbour station and its approaches. As the municipal authorities are happy that the federal government has taken the course of consulting the local authorities each time there is a project to implement, the municipal authorities should now show their satisfaction in giving this policy the high priority and speedy consideration which the federal government has a right to expect, in view of this policy to co-operation and dialogue.
It would be urgent that this construction should start tomorrow, or as soon as possible, in order to prove to the whole Canadian people, to the population of Montreal, and the people of my riding that Liberal promises are not hollow promises. The Minister of Public Works or the Minister of Transport should take the necessary steps so that Montreal's town-planning service may come to a decision. I would even ask, in the event of any undue delay on the part of the city of Montreal, that the plans be drawn up immediately and that the tenders be called as soon as possible, so that this monstrous thing where travellers have to get off may be removed once for all.
The time for conferences is over. The hour for prompt and efficient action has come.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Leblanc) raised this matter during the question period today and directed his question to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin). The hon. member's reason for directing the question to the Minister of Public Works was, I think, because of the action taken by the former minister of public works, the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets). The interest of the former minister of public works' was a personal and local one in that he was member of parliament from the Montreal area, and it was taken on that personal basis and not taken on a departmental basis.
This matter comes within the scope of the national harbours board and consequently inquiries and future action rest with the

Minister of Transport. I can really add nothing more to my reply, and certainly I have no comment to make on the course of action taken by the city of Montreal, as this does not fall within the jurisdiction of the Department of Public Works.

TRADE-SUGGESTED EXPANSION OF CREDIT FOR EXPORT SALES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this afternoon on orders of the day I raised a question with the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It is very difficult on orders of the day to deal in any extended way with matters of this kind and it is for that reason I had it set down for discussion this evening. The question is not in any way critical of the minister who by and large, I think, is one of the more helpful of the frontbenchers in dealing with issues raised by members of the opposition.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: TRADE-SUGGESTED EXPANSION OF CREDIT FOR EXPORT SALES
speechtext: He is the only one on the front bench.

maintopic: TRADE-SUGGESTED EXPANSION OF CREDIT FOR EXPORT SALES
speechtext:
But our export program, and any queries or criticisms which are raised in the public press with regard to it, are so important that it seems to me they should be dealt with and expanded upon at the earliest opportunity. In raising this question I am not suggesting that our present export program in itself is defective. Indeed it has been a considerable success, as the minister pointed out this morning.
But there have been several questions raised in the press lately with regard to the competitive nature of the credit terms extended by Canada and whether or not this is posing a potential danger to the continuing expansion of the export program. The March 20 issue of the Financial Post headlined an article this way: "Are Canada's Export Financing Arrangements Sufficient to Keep Canadian Manufacturers Competitive on World Markets?" The article points out certain examples of changes taking place. It mentions a British exporter who was able to quote 25 year financing terms, whereas our terms are usually 10 years or in some cases as high as 15.
It also points out the new $500 million fund being set up in the United States to undertake export credit financing that is too hazardous for normal commercial undertakings. Then it analyses our present export credit arrangements under section 21(a) and queries whether or not the government should be seriously considering amending or extending this provision so that our exporters will be in a corn-
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion petitive position with regard to other exporters in other parts of the world.
So the first part of my question was a query as to what extent the government has received representations in this field and whether or not it is prepared at this time to make extensions in certainly the terms and length of credit, in order to maintain this competitive position. The other section of the question which I raised is one with regard to which we have been critical in other years with respect to the Export Credits Insurance Corporation, namely its tendency to keep the financing to contracts that are fairly substantial in regard to dollar volume. We have received representations, and I presume the minister has also, that serious thought should be given to financing export credit contracts that are under $2 million, and that this would be beneficial to an expansion in export trade. These are the two points upon which I would like to hear some slight expansion by the minister, so that we may answer these queries which we are receiving.
